💬 Interesting quote from the essay about the insanity that the current reckless race is forcing on the whole world:

> By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. With many dangerous activities, I am fine with somebody doing them for themselves. Wingsuit BASE jumping is dangerous, but I believe in people's freedom to choose that danger, even though they are risking not only their own life, but also hurt to the people who love them. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. And there is no consent from the rest of us. It's as though they're pushing every person in the world off the cliff. The situation is ludicrous.

> In effect, the labs are claiming credit for some imaginary, unquantifiable reduction in risk, while washing their hands of responsibility.

This embodies an extremely naive view that nonetheless a lot of smart people hold: if person X believes Y could be very dangerous then they shouldn't do Y. It's completely naive, because X not doing Y will not make any difference if there are other people/groups who will do Y anyway. If there is no way to stop everyone from doing Y, then you're not adding additional danger to the world by working on it.

And I've never seen any realistic way that you could stop everyone from doing such work on AI. There's too much to be potentially gained from doing so, and there's too many people who don't believe that there actually is great risk to it (and by the way, I'm not one of them)

AND, if you work on it, you can try to make sure that it happens in the safest way possible. If you really think it is potentially dangerous, and there's no way to stop everyone from working on it, then the most responsible thing to do is probably to try to make it happen in the safest way possible.

story.text:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.

I made this game! Some technical details:

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.

There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.

Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.
